name: Hana Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't go with any of it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Pete Dunmore on his hill farm above Elmstead: ninety beef cattle, a hundred acres of hay and a field of oats. I'm there by seven, feeding round bales out of the old Ford tractor and checking the cows for calving signs. In summer it's hay, hay and more hay. I like the views and the quiet, and I don't like the hill in February when the yard turns to ice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I ran the counter at the village shop and post office for eighteen years, till it shut three years ago. Pete needed help after his son moved away, and I'd grown up near cattle, so I asked. I'm still slow at things like reversing a bale trailer, Pete laughs at me. My husband Karl is a lorry mechanic at the haulage yard, and we've got Mia, who's thirteen, Jonas, who's nine, and a bungalow with a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, that's that then, and get on with feeding the cattle. I'm not one for online, I've got a phone that does calls and texts. At the school gate I'd say all that fuss for nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me the trouble was never AI, it's Pete. Pete is sixty-seven, his knees are gone, and he's said twice this year that he might sell up. If Pete Dunmore sells the hill farm, my job goes with the cattle, and no computer needs to be involved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and do as much for Pete as I can, so he keeps going longer. I'd start putting the child benefit aside instead of spending it, so we've got something if the job ends. And I'd ask Karl's boss if the haulage yard ever needs office or cleaning help, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's an old worry. I've been here before with the shop. You can see the end coming and there's nothing you can do to stop it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did losing the shop job teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nobody tells you anything until the week before. The owners knew for a year and I found out from a sign on the door. I'd rather ask Pete straight out than wait for a sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you asked Pete about selling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't. It feels rude, like asking a man about his funeral. I'd do it this winter, though, because I need to know.

say: I'd say it was **all that fuss** for nothing and get on with the cattle.
I'd keep off **online**, since my phone only does calls and texts.
think: I think the real risk is **Pete selling up**, not AI.
I think my job **goes with the cattle** if the farm is sold.
do: Work hard so Pete **keeps going longer**.
Put the **child benefit** aside instead of spending it.
Ask Karl's boss about **office or cleaning** work at the haulage yard.
feel: She feels **worried**, but it's an **old worry** from when the shop shut.
S0.quote: If Pete Dunmore sells the hill farm, my job goes with the cattle, and no computer needs to be involved.
fieldNote: Her job hangs on **Pete's age and knees**, so AI Plateau changes nothing for her.
The **shop closure** taught her that bosses warn late, so she wants to ask Pete directly.
She avoids the question because it feels like asking **about his funeral**.

steps.text: Ask Pete this winter whether he plans to sell
Save the child benefit each month instead of spending it
Ask about cleaning or office shifts at Karl's haulage yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it doesn't touch us up on the hill, and mostly I'd believe it. Pete still writes the cattle movements on a calendar in the kitchen. If it gets into the office jobs, I'd say I'm glad I'm out of the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it touches the people who buy our cattle and sell us our feed, and they'll do it cheaper and faster. That's probably fine for Pete. What bothers me is if a big farm nearby buys robots and makes Pete's way look old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, because I don't see what else I'd do. I wouldn't start using any of these apps, I'd leave that to the kids. Maybe I'd go on the tractor course at the college, because it's practical and it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, like weather coming over the hill. It's not raining yet. I don't like it, but I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Pete use any of the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete might, if his nephew set it up for him. Pete likes anything that saves him paperwork, he just won't admit it. If the computer does Pete's cattle passports, Pete will grumble for a week and then love it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Karl's work at the haulage yard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Karl fixes lorries with his hands, so I'd say he's fine. The office at the yard might shrink, with the bookings and that. That'd be the end of my backup plan, mind.

say: I'd say this **doesn't touch us** up on the hill.
I'd say I'm **glad to be out** of the shop.
think: I think it hits the **cattle buyers** and feed sellers first.
I think a **big robot farm** nearby could make Pete look old-fashioned.
do: Carry on as I am and **leave the apps** to the kids.
Take the **tractor course** at the college, because it's practical.
feel: She feels a bit **uneasy**, like **weather coming** over the hill.
S1.quote: If the computer does Pete's cattle passports, Pete will grumble for a week and then love it.
fieldNote: She'd stay away from AI herself but expects **Pete to love it** once someone sets it up.
Fewer **haulage yard office** jobs would remove her backup plan.
Her mood stays anxious because **Pete selling** remains the threat underneath everything.

steps.text: Take the tractor driving course at the college
Leave the farm apps to Pete's nephew and carry on

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say someone in charge had better have a plan, because I don't. I'm not one for marches, but I'd go to the village meeting if there was one. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, that it's too fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 a robot can feed the cattle and make the hay, and Pete would be seventy-two. Pete would sell to one of the big outfits, and they'd run it with machines. In two years I'd be a forty-five-year-old shop girl with a tractor course and nowhere to drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I could, starting with the second car, and Karl can drop me at the farm. I'd ask my sister in town if we could stay with her if things went bad with the mortgage. I'd look at care work, because everyone says people will still want people for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I'd lie awake doing sums on the back of the electric bill. I'd be short with the kids and hate myself for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Karl's job is hands-on too. Would the robots come for him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably later, I'd hope, because lorries are all different and they break in daft ways. But if the lorries drive themselves, there are fewer to fix. I try not to think too hard about that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia and Jonas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right, because that's what you say. Mia would see through it, Mia always does. I'd tell Mia the truth and ask her to help keep Jonas happy.

say: I'd say someone in charge needs a **plan**, because I don't have one.
I'd go to a **village meeting** and say it's too fast.
think: I think Pete would **sell** to a big outfit that runs on machines.
I think by 2031 I'd have **nowhere to drive** a tractor.
do: Sell the **second car** and get lifts from Karl.
Ask my sister about **staying with her** if the mortgage goes bad.
Look at **care work** as the job people still want people for.
feel: She feels **frightened** and lies awake **doing sums**.
She'd be short with the kids and **hate herself** for it.
S2.quote: In two years I'd be a forty-five-year-old shop girl with a tractor course and nowhere to drive.
fieldNote: The fast picture lands on top of **Pete's age**, so sale and robots arrive together.
Her plans are **defensive**: cut costs, lean on family, look at care work.
She'd trust **Mia, thirteen**, with the truth to help protect Jonas.

steps.text: Sell the second car and share lifts with Karl
Ask my sister about staying with her if needed
Apply for care assistant jobs in Elmstead

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to see it coming, so people should stop pretending it isn't. At the school gate I'd tell the other mums to get the kids into something useful. I'd still not go online about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete's seventy-two in five years, so he'd probably have sold anyway. The robots come in 2034, so whoever buys the farm might keep me a few years, then not. It's the same ending as the fast one, just slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the tractor course and then the care certificate, so I've got two things. I'd keep the child benefit savings going and see if we can get a month or two put by. I'd ask Pete straight out what his plans are, which I should do anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. Less frightened than two years, but I still don't like it. I'd rather have one thing to be good at than two things I'm half good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd rather not use AI tools. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't think so. I'm too set in my ways, and I'd only get it wrong. Give me a sick calf and I'll sit up all night, but give me an app and I'll throw the phone in the trough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need from the government in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something practical, like free courses for grown-ups that run in the evenings. I don't want a handout, I want a hand. And maybe help with the mortgage for a while if the job goes.

say: I'd tell people to **stop pretending** it isn't coming.
I'd tell other mums to get kids into **something useful**.
think: I think Pete would have **sold anyway** by seventy-two.
I think it's the **same ending**, just slower, with a few more years of work.
do: Do the **tractor course** and then the **care certificate**.
Keep saving the **child benefit** to reach a month or two.
Ask Pete straight out about his **plans to sell**.
feel: She feels **uncomfortable** and doubts being **half good** at two things.
S3.quote: Give me a sick calf and I'll sit up all night, but give me an app and I'll throw the phone in the trough.
fieldNote: Five years only delays the outcome, because **Pete's retirement** and the robots line up.
She refuses AI tools even with time, preferring **sick calves to apps**.
She asks for **evening courses** and short mortgage help, not a handout.

steps.text: Take the tractor course, then the care certificate
Keep saving the child benefit to build a cushion
Ask Pete directly about his plans to sell

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and plenty can change. I'd tell people not to panic. That's what I'd say, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years Pete has sold, and I'll have done something else for a while. Mia and Jonas would be grown and gone by the time the robots arrive in 2039. Ten years is long enough that the robots become someone else's problem, maybe the new farmer's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with Pete as long as he farms and do the care certificate on the side. When Pete sells, I'd move to care work in Elmstead for good. I'd keep paying a bit extra on the mortgage whenever there's overtime.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better, though not good. I'm still thinking about Pete's knees more than about robots. Ten years feels like forever and like nothing, both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself at fifty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably at the care home, helping old farmers like Pete. That's a funny thought, isn't it? I'd be fine with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd hold back from changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold back from selling the bungalow. That's ours, and the kids grew up there. I'd cut a lot before I touched that.

say: I'd say ten years is **a long time** and plenty can change.
I'd tell people **not to panic**, whatever I feel.
think: I think Pete will have **sold the farm** well before robots arrive.
I think the kids would be **grown and gone** by 2039.
do: Stay with Pete and take the **care certificate** on the side.
Move to **care work** in Elmstead when Pete sells.
Pay **extra on the mortgage** whenever there's overtime.
feel: She feels better but **not good**, still thinking of **Pete's knees**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that the robots become someone else's problem, maybe the new farmer's.
fieldNote: Her worry stays tied to **Pete's retirement**, which comes long before 2039.
She sees herself in **care work**, helping old farmers, and is at peace with it.
The **bungalow** is the one thing she won't give up.

steps.text: Take the care certificate while still working for Pete
Move into care work in Elmstead when Pete sells
Pay overtime money onto the bungalow mortgage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Pete and the robots would both finish at once, and I'd have nothing lined up. What would help is free evening courses and a few months' help with the mortgage while I find my feet. I don't want a handout, but I'd take a hand up the hill.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about Pete, and he's the one I'd worry about. Pete gave his whole life to that hill. Robots or no robots, Pete will be lost without the cattle.

headlineQuote: I don't want a handout, but I'd take a hand up the hill.
portrait: Hana ran a **village shop counter** for eighteen years before joining Pete Dunmore's hill farm three years ago.
She is **slow with new technology** and refuses AI tools, preferring cattle to apps.
Her real worry is **Pete, sixty-seven**, selling up, which makes her anxious even when AI is hype.
She turns **alarmed** when robots come within five years, with plans to cut costs and move to **care work**.
She's pragmatic, blames nobody, and wants **practical help** rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Pete selling and robots would end her job at once.
whatWouldHelp: Free **evening courses** and a few months of **mortgage help**.
